title: Delivery decisioning vs route optimization: what is the difference?
summary: Route optimization orders a vehicle’s stops. Delivery decisioning chooses which capacity carries each order, and keeps choosing as the day changes.
body_markdown:
Route optimization sequences a vehicle’s stops. Delivery decisioning chooses which capacity carries each order at all, and keeps choosing as conditions change.


**Delivery decisioning** · the whole choice, order to doorstep


Who carries it

route optimization


*·* the one step most operations have already bought


Read for every order · demand · network · reality · learning


## The step that fit in a solver


Route optimization got automated first because its inputs fit. Addresses, time windows, vehicle capacity, a traffic estimate, a service time per stop: the[routing constraints](https://www.nash.ai/glossary/routing-constraint) a solver can hold. Give it those and it returns the best sequence for each vehicle, scored on distance and time. The math has been good for a decade (the solver is not the villain here), and the operator's complaint about it is rarely solver quality (the rules that break routes live in a planner's head, as[a Nash engineer wrote about the gap between the plan and the road](https://www.nash.ai/blog/route-optimization-what-drivers-see) ). The complaint is that the plan answered a narrower question than the one the operation has.


The step underneath · the decisions on top


** Decisions · proposed, approved


STORE-SHIFT


14 orders → neighboring store, pick queue backed up


·proposed


WAVE-MOVED


19 wide-window orders → later wave


·proposed


APPROVED


7 tight-promise orders → courier, cost under the late credit


·dispatcher


Route optimization runs underneath: orders appear, the depot assigns them, each vehicle runs its sequence. The decisions roll on top: which orders leave the fleet, which move store or wave, what a person approves.


The optimizer assumes the set of orders it was handed is the right set. It cannot tell you that order 47 would have been cheaper and faster with a courier, because order 47 was never a candidate. It cannot tell you that the store meant to hand off order 112 is running forty minutes late, because the store's state was never an input. It sequences what it was given. Everything before that, which orders go to which capacity and whether that choice still holds as conditions change, stayed with a person.


## The plan is perfect until it meets the road


Every order has a vehicle. Every vehicle has a sequence. The cost per stop is the lowest the solver could find. If the operation ran the way the plan assumed, this would be the end of the story.


The capacity the plan chooses from is wider than it was. In AlixPartners' 2026 Home Delivery Survey,[more than 90% of logistics and supply chain executives at companies over $100 million in sales said they run a mix of last-mile carriers, and 32% use four or more](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/carrier-diversification-unravels-the-last-mile-delivery-duopoly) . Every added option is another decision the plan froze.


0%


of shippers run four or more last-mile carriers


0%


say per-package delivery costs rose year over year


[AlixPartners, 2026 Home Delivery Survey](https://www.alixpartners.com/insights/annual-home-delivery-survey/)


Then the plan is wrong. A store opens late. A driver calls in. A customer moves their window. A courier network that was cheap when the plan was built is slammed now. None of this is a failure of the optimizer. The inputs changed, and the decision that chose the inputs was made once and frozen.


Most operations absorb this with people. A dispatcher watches the board, catches what they can, and the rest becomes a late delivery and a support ticket. The best dispatchers carry a second plan in their heads: which courier holds up under load, which carrier contract has slack, which store can be trusted to stage on time. Ask them how they decide and they say it depends. It does. The question is what it depends on, and whether any of that lives in software.[Capturing that judgment as rules](https://www.nash.ai/blog/math-and-tribal-knowledge) is the first job, and[putting attention only where the plan broke](https://www.nash.ai/blog/exception-management-filter-not-solver) is the second. Both depend on the decision being made somewhere other than a dispatcher's head.


## What the full decision is made against


A decision is only as good as the context it is made against. The optimizer decides against a thin slice: what customers ordered and a guess at traffic. The full decision about an order needs four kinds of signal.


**Nash Context Fabric** · what every decision is made against


01


*optimizer reads*


### Demand


What was ordered and what was promised.


- the window shown at checkout
- the SLA on the account
- returns and pickups going the other way


02


### Network


What the fulfillment network can do right now.


- drivers on shift
- carrier contracts, courier networks
- what is staged where
- TMS, WMS and ERP, read and written back


03


*optimizer skims*


### Reality


What is happening right now.


- traffic and weather
- a dock closed early, a pickup failed
- a store running behind


04


### Learning


What past deliveries have shown.


- provider reliability under load
- how long an address takes
- demand by season


Lay the two side by side and the subset is plain. Route optimization reads Demand and a little Reality. Delivery decisioning reads all four, for every order, and reads them again when any of them move. The dispatcher's second plan is the Network and Learning signals that were never written down. Nash calls this shared picture the Context Fabric, and it is the reason the rest of the decision can live in software at all.


## Why the order of operations matters


Decide capacity first, then sequence. An order that belongs with a courier should never reach the fleet's optimizer, and an order that belongs on a van should be sequenced with the day's other van orders rather than shipped at parcel rates because the fleet looked full when the plan was built. When the capacity decision is made once a day by rule (everything in zone A to our drivers, overflow to a courier), the optimizer spends its effort polishing a plan built on stale assignments.


Remake the decision continuously and the sequencing step gets better inputs. The courier that was cheap when the plan was built and is slammed now loses the next wave. The store running late loses its hand-offs to a nearby store or a later wave. The van that freed up when a customer cancelled picks up the order that was about to go out at a premium. Each of those is a decisioning change, and each one hands the optimizer a cleaner problem.


The cost shows up in the places the optimizer never measured: the premium courier fee on an order a van could have carried, the failed attempt because the window was never checked against the carrier's cutoff, the support call that followed. In the same AlixPartners survey,[reliability edged past cost as the reason executives choose a primary carrier](https://www.alixpartners.com/insights/annual-home-delivery-survey/) . Both show up as cost problems and are decisioning problems underneath, which is why[cost to serve](https://www.nash.ai/glossary/cost-to-serve) moves when the decision changes and cost per stop does not.


## What it looks like on a dispatch floor


A regional grocer runs its own drivers from twelve stores, with two courier networks for overflow and a 3PL for the long tail. The plan is clean. Then one store reports its pick queue has backed up. Under a frozen decision, its forty orders go out late on the vans that were waiting for them, and a dispatcher starts phoning. Under a decision that is still being made, the orders that can be picked by a neighboring store move there, the ones with wide windows shift to a later wave, and the handful with tight promises go to a courier at a cost the system has already compared against the late-delivery credit. The vans are re-sequenced around what is left. The dispatcher sees the change proposed, with the reasoning, and approves it or doesn't. (The economics of that grocer keeping the order on its own storefront are on the[grocery page](https://www.nash.ai/grocery) .)

None of that is a better route. It is a better decision about which route each order belonged on, made against the state of the store, the carrier, the promise and the price, when the store fell behind rather than when the plan was built.


## Keep the optimizer


The question that comes up most on calls is whether a decisioning layer replaces the routing tool or the TMS. Neither one goes anywhere: the optimizer keeps sequencing stops, the TMS keeps its records and becomes a source of Network signal, and the new layer sits above both, deciding which capacity each order reaches and revisiting that choice as conditions move, which is what[dynamic dispatch](https://www.nash.ai/glossary/dynamic-dispatch) means in practice.[Orchestrate](https://www.nash.ai/orchestrate) is that layer. It makes the decision per order across your own fleet, contracted carriers and a network of more than 250 delivery providers, then carries it through execution and proof of delivery, while[Planning](https://www.nash.ai/planning) does the sequencing on cleaner inputs.[One Platform](https://www.nash.ai/one-platform) shows how the Context Fabric sits under both, and[the autonomic era](https://www.nash.ai/blog/the-autonomic-era-of-logistics) is the longer argument for why the decision has to keep being made.


Route optimization decides the order of a vehicle’s stops. Delivery decisioning decides which capacity carries each order, and keeps deciding as the day changes.


## Delivery decisioning: common questions


01


### Is delivery decisioning the same thing as route optimization?


No. Route optimization is one step inside it: the sequencing of stops for a vehicle once the capacity is chosen. Delivery decisioning covers the whole choice for each order, who carries it, how, and when, and revisits that choice as conditions change.


02


### Does it replace my routing tool?


No. The optimizer keeps the sequencing job. Decisioning sits above it and decides which orders reach it in the first place.


03


### Can it sit on top of an existing TMS?


Yes. The TMS, WMS and carrier systems already in place become sources of Network signal. Decisioning reads from them and writes assignments back rather than replacing them.


04


### How does it choose between my fleet and a carrier?


Per order, by scoring each option on the promise made at checkout, the full cost to serve, the live state of that capacity and its reliability right now. The choice is remade when any of those move.


05


### What does it optimize for?


The promise kept at the lowest cost to serve, which includes the delivery itself, failed attempts, redeliveries and the support contacts that follow. Cost per stop is one line of that.


06


### Where does a dispatcher's judgment go?


Into the rules and preferences the decision is made against, so the second plan a good dispatcher carries in their head becomes an input the system holds continuously. Changes are proposed with their reasoning and approved by a person by default.
